articles.title: Croatia Faces Twin Tests of Credibility: Rising Living Costs and a Toxic Waste Scandal
articles.excerpt: Croatia's government is simultaneously defending its economic record against accusations that price controls mask deeper affordability problems and managing the fallout from a hazardous-waste crisis in Gospić that has provoked parliamentary walkouts and criminal investigations. Together, the two disputes reveal a widening gap between the government's macroeconomic confidence and the daily insecurities felt by ordinary citizens. Both cases carry implications that extend beyond Croatia's borders, touching on EU environmental enforcement and the limits of state intervention in energy markets.

articles.title: Croatia Under Pressure: Toxic Waste Scandal and Stubborn Inflation Test Public Trust in Zagreb
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of Croatians took to the streets of Zagreb to demand action over an illegal hazardous-waste dump exceeding 30,000 tons, as the government faces simultaneous criticism over inflation that remains above the euro-area average. The twin crises are straining public confidence in state institutions and raising questions about Croatia's environmental and economic governance within the European Union. Together, they tell a single story: citizens are questioning whether their government can protect both their environment and their wallets.

articles.title: Croatia Walks a Tightrope Between Resilience and Reform as Inflation Lingers
articles.excerpt: Croatia's economy continues to grow, but slowing momentum and persistent price pressures are testing the government's claim that households are being protected. With inflation projected at 4.6 percent for 2026 and GDP growth forecast to ease to 2.7 percent, Zagreb faces a delicate balancing act between fiscal discipline and public discontent. The country is emerging as a telling case study for the European Union of whether smaller euro-area economies on the periphery can manage growth, disinflation, and budget stability simultaneously.

articles.title: Croatia's Cost-of-Living Squeeze: Fuel Caps and Falling Inflation Figures Mask a Deeper Affordability Crisis
articles.excerpt: Croatia's government has repeatedly intervened to cap retail fuel prices while pointing to easing inflation data as evidence of economic stabilisation. But critics argue that weekly price resets and declining annual rates obscure a more uncomfortable truth: that households are not yet feeling meaningful relief. The gap between official optimism and lived experience is becoming a defining political fault line in Zagreb.

articles.title: Croatia's Inflation Falls but Households Remain Under Pressure as Government Defends Fuel Intervention
articles.excerpt: Croatia's annual inflation slowed to 3.9% in July, offering tentative relief after months of sharp price rises, but the figure still sits well above the European Central Bank's 2% target. The government points to falling headline numbers as proof that its policies are working, while critics argue that everyday costs remain painfully high. A parallel debate over state-mandated fuel price caps is sharpening questions about whether Zagreb is delivering lasting economic stability or merely managing the appearance of one.

articles.title: Croatia Caught Between Political Turbulence and Cost-of-Living Strain
articles.excerpt: Croatia's government is navigating a period of acute institutional stress, as a long-running feud between Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and President Zoran Milanović continues to disrupt policymaking. At the same time, households are still absorbing the effects of elevated prices despite a modest easing of inflation. Together, these pressures are shaping a country that feels, to many of its citizens, perpetually in crisis.

articles.title: Croatia Faces Broad Economic Slowdown as Inflation Keeps Household Budgets Under Strain
articles.excerpt: Croatia's economy is still expanding, but growth is losing momentum across multiple fronts as the European Commission projects a steady deceleration through 2027. At the same time, inflation remains above the euro-area norm, leaving households squeezed even as the government insists the worst of the price shock has passed. Together, the two trends are testing the credibility of the ruling coalition ahead of a period of tighter fiscal conditions.

articles.title: Croatia at a Crossroads: Judicial Pressure and Economic Trade-Offs Test Democratic Norms
articles.excerpt: Croatia is facing a dual challenge that strikes at the heart of its democratic governance: a deepening conflict over judicial independence and a politically charged debate about whether economic relief is being used to sidestep social justice. Both issues have drawn scrutiny from EU institutions and domestic civil society alike. Together, they paint a picture of a country where institutional fatigue is quietly eroding public trust.

articles.title: Croatia's Dual Crisis: Corruption Scandals and Cost-of-Living Anger Test Plenković's Government
articles.excerpt: Croatia is facing simultaneous pressure on two fronts: a politically charged protest wave over judicial appointments and institutional corruption, and growing anger from workers and pensioners over stagnant wages and the cost of living. The appointment of Ivan Turudić as chief state attorney has become a lightning rod for opposition forces and civil society groups pushing for early elections. Together, these developments pose the most serious challenge to Prime Minister Andrej Plenković's ruling Croatian Democratic Union in recent years.

articles.title: Croatia's Twin Pressures: Cost of Living and Labor Shortages Test Economic Resilience
articles.excerpt: Croatia's economy has demonstrated notable resilience in the post-pandemic era, but two structural challenges are testing the limits of that stability: persistent cost-of-living pressure on households and a deepening reliance on foreign workers to fill gaps in the domestic labor market. While headline growth figures remain solid, the gap between macroeconomic performance and everyday experience is widening. Both issues have moved to the center of political debate, with the government and opposition offering starkly different readings of the same data.

articles.title: Croatia's Economic Miracle Has a Credibility Problem
articles.excerpt: Croatia has posted some of the European Union's strongest growth figures in recent years, but a widening gap between official statistics and household experience is fuelling political tension and economic debate. Inflation has eased from its peak, yet the cost-of-living pressure that squeezed ordinary Croatians — particularly lower earners — has left a lasting mark on public trust. The question now is whether Zagreb's post-accession success story is built on durable foundations or a narrow set of fragile growth drivers.

articles.title: Croatia's Economic Miracle Has a Shadow Side: Strong Growth, Stubborn Hardship
articles.excerpt: Croatia has emerged as one of the European Union's more surprising economic success stories, posting strong growth, joining the eurozone, and securing Schengen membership. Yet behind the headline figures lies a more complicated reality: prices remain painfully high for ordinary households, and economists warn that the country's growth model rests on fragile foundations. The gap between official optimism and lived experience is shaping political debate and raising questions about whether Croatia's boom is built to last.

articles.title: Croatia Caught Between Economic Discontent and a Deepening Political Identity Crisis
articles.excerpt: Croatia is navigating a difficult double bind: a cost-of-living squeeze that is eroding public trust in the government's economic narrative, and a widening institutional conflict between Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and President Zoran Milanović over the country's strategic direction. Together, these pressures are testing the cohesion of one of the European Union's newer members at a moment when Brussels demands both fiscal delivery and diplomatic reliability. The stakes extend beyond Zagreb, with implications for EU fund deployment models and the bloc's ability to maintain unified foreign policy among smaller member states.

articles.title: Croatia Faces Twin Threats of Brain Drain and Economic Model Fatigue as EU Integration Honeymoon Fades
articles.excerpt: Three years after joining the eurozone and Schengen Area, Croatia is confronting the unresolved structural weaknesses that EU membership alone cannot fix. A persistent emigration crisis has stripped the country of more than 250,000 residents since 2013, while an economic model built heavily on tourism is showing signs of strain. The political debate over who bears responsibility is growing louder ahead of future electoral contests.

articles.title: Croatia's Growth Story Rings Hollow for Protesters as Inflation Bites Hardest in the Eurozone
articles.excerpt: Thousands of Croatians have taken to the streets of Zagreb demanding higher wages, pensions, and relief from the eurozone's steepest inflation, now running at 4.89% as of March 2026. The protests expose a widening gap between Croatia's solid macroeconomic indicators and the daily financial pressures felt by ordinary citizens. The unrest poses a direct political challenge to Prime Minister Andrej Plenković's government, which points to low unemployment and price controls as evidence of sound management.

articles.title: Croatia's Growth Miracle Hides a Demographic and Fiscal Time Bomb
articles.excerpt: Croatia is posting some of the eurozone's strongest growth figures, but economists and international observers warn that procyclical spending and accelerating population decline are quietly undermining the foundations of that success. The government points to low unemployment and record EU fund absorption as evidence its strategy is working. Critics, backed by IMF data, argue the country is borrowing against a future it may not have the workforce to repay.

articles.title:
Croatia Faces Economic Slowdown as Growth Forecast to Ease
to 2.9 Percent in 2026
articles.excerpt:
Croatia's economy is projected to decelerate from 3.2 percent
growth in 2025 to 2.9 percent in 2026, according to European
Commission forecasts, as household consumption moderates despite
continued EU fund investments. The slowdown comes amid persistent
inflation of 2.8 percent and a widening fiscal deficit expected to
reach 2.9 percent of GDP, testing the government's economic management
ahead of potential electoral contests. While the ruling HDZ party
frames the trajectory as a natural convergence with OECD peers,
opposition voices warn of structural vulnerabilities masked by tourism
revenues and public spending.

articles.title:
Croatia's Political Rift Deepens as EU Funds Drive Growth
Amid Labor Shortages
articles.excerpt:
Croatia's political landscape remains fractured by escalating
tensions between Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and President Zoran
Milanović, complicating foreign policy coordination as the country
navigates EU integration and the Ukraine conflict. Despite persistent
institutional friction and corruption scandals, the economy is
projected to grow 2.9 percent in 2026, fueled by European recovery
funds and an influx of imported labor to offset chronic brain drain.
The dual dynamics of political dysfunction and EU-funded expansion
underscore the challenges facing the Adriatic nation as it seeks
stability within the European bloc.

articles.title:
Croatia's Political Paralysis Deepens as President and Prime
Minister Feud Over Security and Local Power
articles.excerpt:
A bitter rivalry between Croatian President Zoran Milanović
and Prime Minister Andrej Plenković has left key national institutions
in limbo, with the National Security Council dormant for five years
and the Supreme Court without a chief justice for over a year. The
conflict escalated recently when the government overrode Zagreb's
mayor to authorize a controversial concert, sparking accusations of
constitutional violations. The institutional gridlock threatens
Croatia's security readiness and rule of law credentials as the
country approaches the 2028 election cycle.

articles.title:
Croatia Positions Itself as Central European Hub With Twin
Summits on Demographics and Infrastructure
articles.excerpt:
Croatia hosted two major European gatherings in Zagreb this
month, bringing together leaders from the European People's Party and
the Three Seas Initiative to address demographic decline and regional
infrastructure gaps. The summits underscore the country's growing
diplomatic influence within the EU while highlighting tensions between
government ambitions and domestic challenges. Both events carry
significant implications for European energy security, labor markets,
and cross-border connectivity.

articles.title:
CROATIA DEEPENS NATO ROLE WITH TROOP DEPLOYMENTS AND UKRAINE
AID AMID DOMESTIC DEBATE
articles.excerpt:
Croatia is expanding its NATO commitments with troop
deployments to Lithuania, over 300 million euros in Ukraine aid, and
plans to host a 2027 foreign ministers' meeting, NATO Secretary
General Mark Rutte confirmed during a January visit to Zagreb. The
moves strengthen the alliance's eastern flank but have sparked
domestic debate over costs and sovereignty. Separately, Croatia will
host a parliamentary summit of the Three Seas Initiative in 2026,
positioning itself as a regional hub for infrastructure and energy
security.
